claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution produced by standard casting or processing.
Sustained high-amplitude mechanical loading drives elemental segregation along grain boundaries.
Stress-induced grain-boundary segregation leads to nanoscale brittle precipitate formation.
Mechanical loading promotes localized atomic mobility at grain boundaries.
Mechanical loading promotes local compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary compositional fluctuations nucleate brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Brittle grain-boundary precipitates reduce intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion shifts fracture from ductile to brittle behavior.
The proposed grain-boundary degradation lowers overall fracture toughness.
Mechanically stressed specimens will have lower fracture toughness than minimally loaded controls.
Mechanically stressed specimens will exhibit brittle fracture features relative to the baseline.
Chemical mapping of mechanically stressed specimens will reveal grain-boundary elemental segregation.
Microscopy of mechanically stressed specimens will reveal grain-boundary secondary-phase formation.
Minimally loaded baseline samples retain a homogeneous, ductile, single-phase structure with high toughness.
The proposed mechanism dominates above loading-stress and temperature thresholds sufficient to drive significant atomic diffusion.
Below the relevant loading and temperature thresholds, the alloy maintains ductile single-phase behavior.
